sections.title: Introduction to Geometric Optics
objectives: List the ways by which light travels from a source to another location.
summary: List the ways by which light travels from a source to another location.
Explain reflection of light from polished and rough surfaces.
Determine the index of refraction, given the speed of light in a medium.
sections.no_worked_example_reason: The source carries no worked example for this section and no solved exercise to promote, so the practice is left to the exercises themselves.

sections.title: The Ray Aspect of Light
objectives: List the ways by which light travels from a source to another location.

misconceptions.claim: A ray bends towards the normal when it enters glass from air.
misconceptions.correction: It bends away from the normal, because the speed of light is lower in glass.

summary: A straight line that originates at some point is called a ray.
The part of optics dealing with the ray aspect of light is called geometric optics.
Light can travel in three ways from a source to another location: (1) directly from the source through empty space; (2) through various media; (3) after being reflected from a mirror.

sections.title: The Law of Reflection
objectives: Explain reflection of light from polished and rough surfaces.
summary: The angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence.
A mirror has a smooth surface and reflects light at specific angles.
Light is diffused when it reflects from a rough surface.

sections.title: The Law of Refraction
objectives: Determine the index of refraction, given the speed of light in a medium.

misconceptions.claim: A converging lens forms an image at the same place whatever the object distance.
misconceptions.correction: The image distance changes with the object distance, and the lens equation gives it.

summary: The changing of a light ray’s direction when it passes through variations in matter is called refraction.
The speed of light in vacuum c=2.99792458×108 m/s≈3.00×108 m/s.
Index of refraction n=cv, where v is the speed of light in the material, c is the speed of light in vacuum, and n is the index of refraction.

sections.title: Total Internal Reflection
objectives: Explain the phenomenon of total internal reflection.
Describe the workings and uses of fiber optics.
Analyze the reason for the sparkle of diamonds.
summary: The incident angle that produces an angle of refraction of 90º is called critical angle.

Total internal reflection is a phenomenon that occurs at the boundary between two mediums, such that if the incident angle in the first medium is greater than the critical angle, then all the light is reflected back into that medium.
Fiber optics involves the transmission of light down fibers of plastic or glass, applying the principle of total internal reflection.

sections.title: Dispersion: The Rainbow and Prisms
objectives: Explain the phenomenon of dispersion and discuss its advantages and disadvantages.
summary: The spreading of white light into its full spectrum of wavelengths is called dispersion.
Rainbows are produced by a combination of refraction and reflection and involve the dispersion of sunlight into a continuous distribution of colors.
Dispersion produces beautiful rainbows but also causes problems in certain optical systems.

sections.title: Image Formation by Lenses
objectives: List the rules for ray tracing for thin lenses.
Illustrate the formation of images using the technique of ray tracing.
Determine power of a lens given the focal length.
summary: Light rays entering a converging lens parallel to its axis cross one another at a single point on the opposite side.
For a converging lens, the focal point is the point at which converging light rays cross; for a diverging lens, the focal point is the point from which diverging light rays appear to originate.
The distance from the center of the lens to its focal point is called the focal length f.

sections.title: Image Formation by Mirrors
objectives: Illustrate image formation in a flat mirror.
Explain with ray diagrams the formation of an image using spherical mirrors.
Determine focal length and magnification given radius of curvature, distance of object and image.
summary: The characteristics of an image formed by a flat mirror are: (a) The image and object are the same distance from the mirror, (b) The image is a virtual image, and (c) The image is situated behind the mirror.
Image length is half the radius of curvature. f=R2
A convex mirror is a diverging mirror and forms only one type of image, namely a virtual image.

exam_traps.correction: It bends away from the normal, because the speed of light is lower in glass.

exam_traps.subject: physics
exam_traps.misconception: A converging lens forms an image at the same place whatever the object distance.
exam_traps.correction: The image distance changes with the object distance, and the lens equation gives it.
exam_traps.signal: Our own teaching of the section, waiting for a paper question that shows the same mistake.

exam_traps.subject: physics
exam_traps.misconception: The law of reflection says the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence, both measured from the surface.
exam_traps.correction: Both angles are measured from the normal, the line perpendicular to the surface at the point of incidence. Measuring from the surface gives a different pair of numbers, though the two are complementary.
exam_traps.signal: Our own question asks which angle the reflection angle equals.

exam_traps.subject: physics
exam_traps.misconception: Snell's law relates the angles of incidence and refraction to the wavelengths in the two media.
exam_traps.correction: It relates them to the speeds of light, through the refractive indices. The wavelengths change as the speed changes, and the frequency does not, which is the point of the law.
exam_traps.signal: Our own question offers the wavelength reading as an option.
